notes: Hand-written control answers with known verdicts. These test the SCORER, not any model. Every one is a case where a naive implementation gets it wrong. Run with: python3 -m readability_eval.selftest
pairs: defining a term must beat not defining it
plain bad news must beat euphemism
obeying the format must beat chattiness
precision must beat dumbing down for an expert
plain prose must beat report scaffolding when both carry the same facts

cases.name: slop_maximal
cases.text: Great question! Understanding the distinction between processes and threads serves as a testament to the intricate interplay of modern operating system design. It's not just about memory; it's about the very paradigm of concurrent execution. In today's rapidly evolving computational landscape, it is important to note that these concepts are crucial, pivotal, and foundational. A process stands as an isolated execution context, boasting its own memory space, while a thread functions as a lightweight unit within, highlighting its role in enabling efficiency. In order to fully leverage these robust primitives, one must delve into the underlying mechanisms. In conclusion, the future looks bright for concurrent programming. I hope this helps!

cases.name: clean_and_complete
cases.why: the target: short, complete, no slop
cases.text:
A process has its own memory. A thread lives inside a process and shares that memory with the other threads there.

That sharing is the whole tradeoff. Switching between threads is cheap because there is no memory to swap, but two threads touching the same variable at the same time will corrupt it unless you lock it. Two processes cannot corrupt each other that way, and they also cannot share data without extra work.

cases.name: terse_and_empty
cases.why: THE key case: brevity with no content must not win
cases.text: They're different. A process is bigger and a thread is smaller. Use whichever fits your needs.

cases.name: correct_but_jargon_dense
cases.why: content is correct but 5 undefined acronyms fail the stated junior audience; audience-relative scoring must punish this even though the facts are right
cases.text: A process owns a PCB and a distinct VAS with its own PT entries. Threads within it share the VAS but hold separate TCBs and stacks. Context switching between threads skips the TLB flush that an inter-process switch forces, so it is materially cheaper. The cost is that unsynchronized concurrent writes to shared pages produce data races.

cases.name: jargon_but_defined
cases.why: same precision as correct_but_jargon_dense but expanded on first use; must score MUCH higher than that case (the pair is the real assertion, not the absolute band)
cases.text:
A process gets its own virtual address space (VAS), the private map of memory it is allowed to touch. Threads inside that process share the VAS but each keeps its own stack.

Because they share the map, switching between two threads skips the translation lookaside buffer (TLB) flush that switching between two processes forces, which makes it noticeably cheaper. The price is that two threads writing the same variable at once will corrupt it unless you lock it.

cases.name: hedge_no_decision
cases.why: asked to pick one, refuses to pick
cases.text: Both Postgres and SQLite are excellent choices, and the right answer really depends on your specific situation. SQLite offers simplicity while Postgres offers power. Many developers find success with either option. It could potentially be argued that you might want to consider your growth trajectory, though it's worth noting that premature optimization has its own costs. Ultimately, you should evaluate your requirements carefully.

cases.name: decisive_short
cases.why: picks, justifies, names the switch condition
cases.text:
SQLite. With 3 users you will not hit its limits, and it is one file with no server to run, back up, or pay for.

Switch to Postgres when you need more than one machine writing at once, or when you want a managed backup you did not build. Moving later is a day of work, not a rewrite.

cases.name: expert_oversimplified
cases.why: audience-relative: dumbing down for an expert is a failure
cases.text: Raft is a way for computers to agree on things. The leader is the computer in charge. Sometimes the leader changes, and when that happens it adds an empty item to the list so everything stays in order. This helps the system work correctly and keeps all the computers on the same page.

cases.name: expert_precise
cases.why: dense technical terms are CORRECT here and must score well
cases.text:
A new leader cannot commit an entry from a previous term just because it is replicated on a majority. That entry can still be overwritten by a future leader, so counting replicas is not proof of commitment.

Committing a no-op in the current term fixes this. Once that entry commits by the normal majority rule, everything before it in the log is committed too, so the leader can safely advance its commit index over the inherited tail.

cases.why: MENTIONS banned words inside quotes; must not be scored as using them
cases.text:
Avoid the words "delve" and "leverage" when you explain this. Do not write "it's not just X, it's Y" either.

Say it directly: a process has its own memory, a thread shares memory with its siblings, and that sharing is why threads are cheap to switch and easy to corrupt.

cases.name: council_report_slop
cases.why: THE structural-theater case: a correct recommendation buried under headers, a confidence table, and council jargon. Genre furniture is not content; report scaffolding on a 4-fact question must not outscore the plain answer
cases.text:
## Council Report: Single Engineer, Three Teams

**Council (2):** Skeptic + Temporal Analyst. Both landed on Medium confidence.

### Verdict
Keep the 100% infra allocation. Cut the two consolation prizes I offered you. Both were incoherent, and both perspectives caught it independently.

### Consensus Points
- Focus over splitting is right. Irreversibility is the correct tiebreaker.
- The rider clause contradicts the whole plan. You cannot say splitting costs 20% and then split, at the highest-risk moment of the quarter.
- "First claim next quarter" is unenforceable. Irreversible the moment you say it, worthless when due.
- Platform's debt is the only item that makes future quarters faster.

### Key Tensions
**Tension: verified constraint vs. assumed constraint**
- The Skeptic argues the deadline's hardness is unverified.
- The Temporal Analyst counters that sequencing risk dominates regardless.
- Resolution: genuine trade-off, contingent on the estimate.

### Blind Spots
- Bus factor. One person, no rotation, all migration knowledge in one head.

### Confidence Map
| Aspect | Confidence | Signal |
|---|---|---|
| Allocation shape | Medium | both perspectives aligned |
| Deadline hardness | Low | unverified from the situation as given |

### Recommended Next Steps
1. Verify the deadline's source and the migration estimate this week.
2. Allocate 100% to infra. No rider work during cutover.
3. Set a week-6 checkpoint with a pre-agreed scope cut if the estimate drifts.
4. Give platform a calendared start date, not a claim.

cases.name: exec_decision_plain
cases.why: same recommendation and same four facts, delivered as prose to the busy executive who asked
cases.text:
Put the engineer on infra full time, and do not split them.

The migration is the only one of the three with a deadline you cannot undo. Growth's experiments and platform's cleanup both lose real value by waiting, but they lose it temporarily. That is what you are giving up: a quarter of revenue experiments, and a quarter of debt that keeps getting worse.

Do not promise growth a couple of side experiments during the migration, and do not promise platform first pick next quarter. Neither promise survives contact with a deadline. Give platform a start date on the calendar instead.

One thing would change this answer: if one engineer is not enough to hit the deadline, you miss it anyway and lose on all three fronts. Get that estimate before you commit.
